question.text: Implement a complete C++17 bounded FIFO of capacity 17 with overflow rejection, push, pop, and a test main that fills, overflows, drains, and wraps around. Explain the invariant before writing the code.
Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?

allJobs.answer:
Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time. Each transaction checks its own consistent snapshot, and ordinary snapshot isolation detects conflicting writes to the same row—not every conflict between what one transaction reads and another writes.

For example, suppose Alice and Bob are both on call, and the rule is that at least one must remain on call. Two concurrent transactions each read that both are on call; one then marks Alice off call, while the other marks Bob off call. Because they update different rows, both can commit, leaving nobody on call even though each check passed.

Atomicity guarantees that each transaction’s changes happen entirely or not at all; it does not guarantee that its check remains valid against concurrent changes. Preventing this write skew requires serializable isolation or an explicit locking or shared-write scheme that forces these transactions to conflict.

question.text: Your bounds separated observations from assumptions

Switch to cooling two kilograms of well mixed water starts at sixty degrees Celsius in a room held at twenty degrees It reaches forty degrees after ten minutes and thirty after twenty specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Vessel heat capacity is negligible no evaporation or internal heating occurs Heat loss power equals constant conductance times water temperature minus room temperature derive conductance with units interviewer pause one point five seconds A later run starts at sixty and reaches twenty seven after twenty minutes its constant ambient temperature was not logged Construct two exact explanations one retaining conductance and one retaining twenty degree ambient What experiment distinguishes them

allJobs.answer:
The original conductance is 14 ln(2) watts per kelvin, approximately 9.70 W/K. The later result can be explained exactly either by a colder room at 16°C with that same conductance, or by increased conductance at a room temperature of 20°C.

The water’s heat capacity is C = mc = 2 × 4,200 = 8,400 J/K. Conservation of energy gives
C dT/dt = −G(T − A),
where G is conductance and A is constant ambient temperature. Integrating gives
T(t) = A + (T(0) − A) exp(−Gt/C),
with time in seconds.

In the original run, the temperature excess above 20°C falls from 40 K to 20 K in 600 seconds, so
exp(−600G/8,400) = 1/2,
G = (8,400/600) ln(2) = 14 ln(2) W/K.
At twenty minutes the excess is one quarter of its initial value, predicting 20 + 40/4 = 30°C, consistent with the second observation.

For the later run, here are two exact explanations:

1. Retain the original conductance. Its twenty-minute decay factor remains 1/4. Therefore
27 = A + (60 − A)/4,
which gives A = 16°C.

2. Retain the 20°C ambient temperature. Then
27 − 20 = (60 − 20) exp(−1,200G/8,400),
so
G = 7 ln(40/7) W/K ≈ 12.20 W/K.
This is about 26% greater than the original conductance.

To distinguish them, repeat the later setup while continuously measuring both ambient and water temperatures, preferably holding the ambient at a verified 20°C. Under the unchanged-conductance explanation, the water reaches 30°C after twenty minutes; under the increased-conductance explanation, it reaches 27°C. Fit the logged cooling curve to check conductance and whether the constant-ambient model actually holds. The single later endpoint alone cannot identify both ambient temperature and conductance, and a repeat only diagnoses the earlier run if its heat-transfer conditions are reproduced.

allJobs.answer:
Because cooling depends on both conductance and ambient temperature, the later endpoint alone cannot tell us which changed.

The water’s heat capacity is C = mc = 2 × 4,200 = 8,400 J/K. Energy conservation gives C dT/dt = −G(T − A), so T(t) = A + (60 − A)e^(−Gt/C), with time in seconds. In the original run, the temperature excess above 20°C halves in 600 seconds, giving G = (8,400/600) ln 2 = 14 ln 2 ≈ 9.70 W/K. That also predicts 30°C at twenty minutes, matching the second observation.

For the later run, retaining that conductance makes the twenty-minute decay factor exactly 1/4. Thus 27 = A + (60 − A)/4, which gives A = 16°C. Alternatively, retaining A = 20°C gives 7 = 40e^(−1,200G/8,400), so G = 7 ln(40/7) ≈ 12.20 W/K. Both explanations reproduce 27°C exactly.

To distinguish them, measure the ambient temperature during a repeat under the later run’s conditions: the explanations predict 16°C versus 20°C. An additional water-temperature measurement at ten minutes also distinguishes these two models: they predict 38°C versus 20 + √280 ≈ 36.73°C, provided the conditions remain unchanged.

allJobs.answer: Warp divergence can reduce performance because a warp cannot execute different branch instructions simultaneously for different threads. It executes each required path with threads that don’t belong to that path masked off, then reconverges. That leaves some lanes inactive during each path, reducing useful work compared with all 32 threads following the same path.

question.text: Here, “route” means a minimum-cost walk from vertex s to vertex t in a directed graph. Integer weights may be negative; walks may repeat edges and vertices. Parallel edges and self-loops are allowed. [pause] Write executable Python 3 classify_route(n, edges, s, t), returning a pair: status and cost. Status is UNREACHABLE, FINITE, or UNBOUNDED; cost is an integer only for FINITE, otherwise None. UNBOUNDED means arbitrarily negative costs are possible. Vertices are zero-based; n is between one and two thousand, edges number at most ten thousand, and absolute weights are at most one trillion. Give an invariant and justified worst-case time and memory bounds. Which negative cycles affect this query?

ear Root means a minimum cost walk from vertex S to vertex T in a directed graph integer weights may be negative walks may repeat edges and vertices parallel edges and self loops are allowed pause right executable Python three classify underscore root N edges s T returning a pair status and cost status is unreachable finite or unbounded cost is an integer only for finite otherwise none unbounded means are arbitrarily negative costs are possible vertices are zero based N is between one and two thousand edge is number at most ten thousand and absolute weights are at most one trillion given invariant and justified worst case time and memory bounds which negative cycles affect this query

allJobs.answer:
Only negative cycles reachable from S and able to reach T make this query unbounded. A negative cycle elsewhere does not affect the answer. I’m interpreting the spoken identifier as `classify_route(n, edges, s, t)` and “route” as a walk, so repeated vertices and edges are allowed.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys


def classify_route(n, edges, s, t):
    """Return (status, cost) for the minimum-cost s-to-t walk.

    edges contains (u, v, weight) triples with integer weights.
    Vertices are numbered 0 through n - 1.
    """
    edges = list(edges)
    forward = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    reverse = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, weight in edges:
        forward[u].append(v)
        reverse[v].append(u)

    def reachable(start, adjacency):
        seen = [False] * n
        seen[start] = True
        stack = [start]
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            for v in adjacency[u]:
                if not seen[v]:
                    seen[v] = True
                    stack.append(v)
        return seen

    from_s = reachable(s, forward)
    if not from_s[t]:
        return ("unreachable", None)

    to_t = reachable(t, reverse)
    relevant = [from_s[v] and to_t[v] for v in range(n)]
    k = sum(relevant)
    useful_edges = [
        (u, v, weight)
        for u, v, weight in edges
        if relevant[u] and relevant[v]
    ]

    # Synchronous Bellman-Ford: each round adds at most one edge.
    dist = [None] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    for round_number in range(1, k + 1):
        next_dist = dist.copy()
        changed = False
        for u, v, weight in useful_edges:
            if dist[u] is None:
                continue
            candidate = dist[u] + weight
            if next_dist[v] is None or candidate < next_dist[v]:
                next_dist[v] = candidate
                changed = True

        if not changed:
            return ("finite", dist[t])
        if round_number == k:
            return ("unbounded", None)
        dist = next_dist

    raise AssertionError("Unreachable control path")


def main():
    # Input: n m s t, followed by m triples: u v weight.
    tokens = iter(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n = next(tokens)
    m = next(tokens)
    s = next(tokens)
    t = next(tokens)
    edges = [(next(tokens), next(tokens), next(tokens))
             for _ in range(m)]
    status, cost = classify_route(n, edges, s, t)
    print(status, cost if cost is not None else "None")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run with Python 3, for example `python3 route.py < input.txt`. The function itself returns the requested pair; the command-line wrapper prints it.

Correctness invariant: after round r, `dist[v]` is the minimum cost of any S-to-v walk using at most r edges in the relevant subgraph, or `None` if no such walk exists. Initially only the zero-edge walk to S exists. Each round copies the previous distances and relaxes edges using only the previous array, so it considers exactly the old walks plus their one-edge extensions.

Every S-to-T walk lies entirely in the relevant subgraph: each vertex on it is reachable from S and can reach T. Conversely, every retained vertex is reachable from S within that subgraph and can reach T within it.

If there is no negative cycle in this subgraph, removing cycles from any walk never increases its cost. Thus a minimum-cost path uses at most k−1 edges, where k is the number of relevant vertices, and round k cannot improve any distance. If a round makes no change, the distances are a fixed point, so returning the finite distance is safe.

If round k improves a distance, there must be a reachable negative cycle: otherwise all minimum distances would already have been attained using at most k−1 edges. Conversely, a reachable negative cycle prevents a fixed point, because the inequalities `dist[v] <= dist[u] + weight` around that cycle would imply zero is at most its negative total weight. Since every retained cycle can reach T, repeating it arbitrarily many times and then continuing to T gives arbitrarily negative costs.

This also handles parallel edges, self-loops, and S equal to T. In that last case the empty walk has cost zero, unless a reachable negative cycle can return to S.

Worst-case time is O(n + m + k(n + m_relevant)), hence O(n(n + m)); memory is O(n + m). There are at most 2,000 rounds and 20 million edge examinations under the supplied limits. Every computed distance represents a walk of at most k edges, so its magnitude is at most k × 10^12, or 2 × 10^15; Python integers handle these exactly.

Save it in a Python 3 module and call it with an iterable of edge triples, for example:

```python

assert classify_root(2, [], 0, 1) == ("unreachable", None)
assert classify_root(2, [(0, 0, -1), (0, 1, 7)], 0, 1) == (
```

The invariant is that after round k, each distance is the minimum cost of a walk from S to that vertex using at most k edges in the relevant subgraph; None means no such walk exists. Each round copies the previous distances and relaxes only from that previous array, so it either keeps a shorter walk or appends exactly one edge. This establishes the invariant by induction.

Every vertex in the relevant subgraph is reachable from S and can reach T. Those connecting paths also stay in the subgraph. Therefore, any negative cycle in it can be reached, repeated arbitrarily many times, and followed by a path to T, making the query unbounded.

A minimum-cost walk can therefore be chosen as a simple path with at most K−1 edges. Distances must stabilize by then, so an improvement in round K proves a relevant negative cycle exists. If any earlier round has no improvement, the distances are a fixed point and the result is finite. When S equals T, the empty walk has cost zero, but a reachable negative cycle that can return to S still makes the result unbounded. Parallel edges and self-loops require no special handling.

With M edges, reachability costs O(N+M). question.text: Your exact-integer argument avoids overflow; abruptly switch to numerical analysis. Python 3 floats here use IEEE 754 binary64, round-to-nearest ties-to-even, with gradual underflow. Implement f(x) for every finite nonnegative float x, approximating square root of x squared plus one, minus x. Direct evaluation suffers cancellation and overflow. [pause] Your result must remain positive even at x equal to ten to the power 308. You may use math.hypot, assumed correctly rounded. Give executable code, justify every intermediate's range, and derive a relative-error bound where the exact result is normal. What guarantee remains when it is subnormal?

allJobs.answer:
Rationalize the expression, then halve the denominator before adding: this avoids both cancellation and overflow, and remains positive even at x = 10**308.

```python
import math

def f(x):
    """Approximate sqrt(x*x + 1) - x for finite nonnegative binary64 x."""
    if not math.isfinite(x) or x < 0.0:
        raise ValueError("x must be finite and nonnegative")
    h = math.hypot(x, 1.0)
    d = 0.5 * h + 0.5 * x
    return 0.5 / d
```

Use Python 3 with the stated binary64 semantics and correctly rounded math.hypot; no additional dependencies are needed.

The exact identity is
    y = sqrt(x² + 1) − x = 1 / (sqrt(x² + 1) + x).
Writing H = sqrt(x² + 1) and D = (H + x)/2 gives y = 0.5/D. The code never forms x² or H + x.

Here are the intermediate ranges. Let F be the largest finite binary64 number. Correctly rounded hypot produces 1 ≤ h ≤ F. Even at x = F, the exact H exceeds F by only 1/(H + F), far below the overflow-rounding threshold, so h remains finite. Multiplication of h by 0.5 is exact and lies between 0.5 and F/2. Multiplication of x by 0.5 lies between zero and F/2; only this multiplication can underflow. Their rounded sum lies between 0.5 and F, so it cannot overflow or be zero. The exact final quotient therefore lies between 0.5/F and 1. In particular, its lower bound is about 2.78 × 10⁻³⁰⁹, enormously larger than the smallest subnormal, so rounding cannot produce zero. At x = 10**308 the result is approximately 5 × 10⁻³⁰⁹.

For an explicit error bound, set u = 2⁻⁵³ and η = 2⁻¹⁰⁷⁴, the smallest positive subnormal. Correct rounding gives |h − H| ≤ uH. Halving h is exact. Halving x is also exact unless it enters the subnormal range, where its absolute error is at most η/2. Since D ≥ 0.5, that error is certainly at most uD. Consequently the unrounded denominator differs from D by at most 2uD. The denominator addition rounds a normal result, giving
    |d/D − 1| ≤ e, where e = 3u + 2u².
This is a conservative bound, not a tight one.

Before rounding the division, q = 0.5/d satisfies
    |q/y − 1| ≤ e/(1 − e).
If the exact result y is normal, division rounding has absolute error at most u·max(q, minimum_normal). Both entries in that maximum are at most y/(1 − e), even if q crosses just below the normal boundary. Thus the returned result satisfies
    |f(x)/y − 1| ≤ (e + u)/(1 − e),
which is approximately 4u, or 4.45 × 10⁻¹⁶.

When y is subnormal, the usual uniform relative rounding bound of u no longer applies. An always-valid absolute bound is
    |f(x) − y| ≤ ((e + u)/(1 − e))·y + η/2.
Equivalently, the relative bound has the additional term η/(2y). Gradual underflow preserves this absolute-error guarantee, and the range argument above independently guarantees a strictly positive return for every allowed x.

Only negative cycles reachable from S and able to reach T make this query unbounded. I’m interpreting “root” as the minimum-cost walk you defined, while keeping the requested identifier `classify_root`. Use reachability to isolate the relevant vertices, then run Bellman–Ford on that subgraph.

```python
from collections import deque


def classify_root(N, edges, S, T):
    """Return (status, cost) for the minimum-cost S-to-T walk.

    Vertices are 0..N-1; edges contains (u, v, integer_weight).
    Status is 'unreachable', 'finite', or 'unbounded'.
    The empty walk is allowed when S == T.
    """
    edges = list(edges)
    adj = [[] for _ in range(N)]
    rev = [[] for _ in range(N)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        rev[v].append(u)

    def reachable(start, graph):
        seen = [False] * N
        seen[start] = True
        queue = deque([start])
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            for v in graph[u]:
                if not seen[v]:
                    seen[v] = True
                    queue.append(v)
        return seen

    from_s = reachable(S, adj)
    if not from_s[T]:
        return ('unreachable', None)

    to_t = reachable(T, rev)
    relevant = [from_s[v] and to_t[v] for v in range(N)]
    K = sum(relevant)
    filtered = [(u, v, w) for u, v, w in edges
                if relevant[u] and relevant[v]]

    dist = [None] * N
    dist[S] = 0

    for _ in range(K - 1):
        changed = False
        for u, v, w in filtered:
            if dist[u] is None:
                continue
            candidate = dist[u] + w
            if dist[v] is None or candidate < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = candidate
                changed = True
        if not changed:
            return ('finite', dist[T])

    # Test without updating: any remaining improvement proves
    # a negative cycle in the relevant subgraph.
    for u, v, w in filtered:
        if dist[u] is not None:
            candidate = dist[u] + w
            if dist[v] is None or candidate < dist[v]:
                return ('unbounded', None)

    return ('finite', dist[T])
```

Run this with Python 3; no third-party packages are needed. For example, `classify_root(2, [(0, 1, -7)], 0, 1)` returns `('finite', -7)`.

Correctness and invariant:

• Every vertex on an S-to-T walk is reachable from S and can reach T, so filtering removes no possible answer. Conversely, every retained vertex is reachable from S within the retained subgraph.

• Every non-None distance is the cost of an actual walk from S. After pass j, the distance at each vertex is no greater than the cost of any path to it using at most j edges. In-place updates may propagate farther in a pass, but do not invalidate either property.

• Without a relevant negative cycle, cycles can be removed from a minimum-cost walk without increasing its cost. Therefore an optimum has at most K−1 edges, and after K−1 passes the distances are exact. An early pass with no changes is also safe: all edge inequalities already hold.

• After K−1 passes all retained vertices have finite distances. If a further edge can improve a distance, the no-negative-cycle conclusion above is impossible, so a relevant negative cycle exists. Conversely, if a negative cycle exists, not all its edge inequalities can hold: summing them would imply that its total weight is nonnegative. Thus the final test detects it.

A relevant negative cycle can be reached from S, traversed arbitrarily many times, and then left along a path to T, making costs arbitrarily negative. A negative cycle unreachable from S, or unable to reach T, does not affect this query. This also handles negative self-loops, parallel edges, and S equal to T; in the last case the empty walk costs zero unless a relevant negative cycle makes the answer unbounded.

Worst-case bounds: let M be the number of supplied edges and M_r the number retained. Reachability and filtering take O(N + M) time; relaxation takes O(K M_r), giving O(N + M + NM) total time and O(N + M) auxiliary memory. Under your limits, relaxation examines at most 2,000 × 10,000 = 20,000,000 edges, including the final check. Python integers avoid overflow; distance magnitudes are bounded by roughly K M_r × 10^12 during these in-place passes, so arithmetic remains on small, bounded-size integers for the stated limits.

```python
    edges contains (source, destination, integer_weight) triples.
    status is 'unreachable', 'finite', or 'unbounded'.

    reverse = [[] for _ in range(N)]

        reverse[v].append(u)

                    queue.append(v)

        return ('unreachable', None)
```
